## Software construction

SWEBOK (the *Software Engineering Body of Knowledge*, published by IEEE) defines it as:

>Software construction refers to the detailed creation and maintenance of software through coding, verification, unit testing, integration testing and debugging.[^swebok-definition]

[^swebok-definition]: [SWEBOK Guide v4.0](https://www.computer.org/education/bodies-of-knowledge/software-engineering) (IEEE Computer Society, 2024), chapter 4 "Software Construction", p. 4-1.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    Requirements --> Design
    Design --> Construction
    Construction -->|release| Users
    Users -->|feedback, new needs| Requirements
    classDef focus stroke-width:3px
    class Construction focus
```

### How SWEBOK is organized

- **18 knowledge areas**[^swebok-kas]: requirements, architecture, design, **construction**, testing, operations, maintenance, configuration management, management, process, models and methods, quality, security, professional practice, economics, and three foundations (computing, mathematical, engineering).
- Every knowledge area is a hierarchy of **topics**. The first topic is the area's **fundamentals** - the principles everything else builds on.
- Software Construction[^swebok-construction-topics]: 1. Fundamentals, 2. Managing construction, 3. Practical considerations, 4. Construction technologies, 5. Tools.

[^swebok-kas]: [SWEBOK Guide v4.0](https://www.computer.org/education/bodies-of-knowledge/software-engineering), Introduction, Table I.1 "The 18 SWEBOK KAs".
[^swebok-construction-topics]: [SWEBOK Guide v4.0](https://www.computer.org/education/bodies-of-knowledge/software-engineering), chapter 4, "Breakdown of topics for Software Construction".

### Construction fundamentals

SWEBOK lists five fundamentals of software construction[^swebok-fundamentals]:

1. **Minimizing complexity** - code that people can understand.
1. **Anticipating and embracing change** - code that can be changed cheaply.
1. **Constructing for verification** - code in which faults are easy to find.
1. **Reusing assets** - using existing assets, and creating reusable ones.
1. **Applying standards in construction** - agreeing on how code is written, and enforcing it.

[^swebok-fundamentals]: [SWEBOK Guide v4.0](https://www.computer.org/education/bodies-of-knowledge/software-engineering), section 4.1 "Software Construction Fundamentals", pp. 4-2 – 4-4.

## Measuring construction

### Goal, question, metric

A metric is useful only when it answers a question that matters. The *Goal-Question-Metric* approach[^gqm] starts from the goal:

[^gqm]: V. Basili, G. Caldiera, H. D. Rombach, ["The Goal Question Metric Approach"](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~mvz/handouts/gqm.pdf), Encyclopedia of Software Engineering, 1994.

| Goal | Question | Metric |
|---|---|---|
| Adding experience rules should take hours, not days | Which code is hardest to understand? | Cyclomatic complexity |
| | Which code changes most often? | Churn |
| Bugs should be caught before release | Would the tests notice a wrong rule? | Mutation score |
| Dependencies should not put users at risk | Do we ship known vulnerabilities? | Vulnerable packages |

### What SWEBOK suggests to measure

>Numerous construction activities and artifacts can be measured, including code developed, modified, reused, and destroyed; code complexity; code inspection statistics; fault-fix and fault-find rates; effort; and scheduling.[^swebok-measurement]

[^swebok-measurement]: [SWEBOK Guide v4.0](https://www.computer.org/education/bodies-of-knowledge/software-engineering), section 4.2.3 "Construction Measurement", p. 4-5.

### Goodhart's law

>When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.[^goodhart]

Every code metric can be gamed. Rules of thumb that keep metrics useful:

- Use a metric as a question in a code review, not as a verdict.[^space]
- Watch trends, not absolute values: is the code getting better or worse?[^tornhill]
- Compare numbers only from the same tool: tools count differently (an example is in [Reducing complexity](#reducing-complexity)).
- Measure what changed in a pull request, not the whole codebase at once.[^clean-as-you-code]

[^goodhart]: Marilyn Strathern's 1997 wording of [Goodhart's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodhart%27s_law); Charles Goodhart's original (1975) was about monetary policy.
[^space]: N. Forsgren, M.-A. Storey et al., ["The SPACE of Developer Productivity"](https://doi.org/10.1145/3454122.3454124), ACM Queue, 2021; N. Forsgren, J. Humble, G. Kim, [*Accelerate*](https://itrevolution.com/product/accelerate/), 2018.
[^tornhill]: A. Tornhill, [*Your Code as a Crime Scene*](https://pragprog.com/titles/atcrime2/your-code-as-a-crime-scene-second-edition/), 2nd ed., 2024.
[^clean-as-you-code]: SonarSource, ["Clean as You Code"](https://docs.sonarsource.com/sonarqube-server/latest/core-concepts/clean-as-you-code/introduction/).

## Minimizing complexity

### What is complexity

>Complexity is anything related to the structure of a software system that makes it hard to understand and modify the system.
>
>John Ousterhout[^aposd]

[^aposd]: J. Ousterhout, [*A Philosophy of Software Design*](https://web.stanford.edu/~ouster/cgi-bin/aposd.php), chapter 2 "The Nature of Complexity".

>Most people have limited ability to hold complex structures and information in their working memories, especially over long periods.
>
>SWEBOK[^swebok-complexity]

[^swebok-complexity]: [SWEBOK Guide v4.0](https://www.computer.org/education/bodies-of-knowledge/software-engineering), section 4.1.1 "Minimizing Complexity", p. 4-2.

### Working memory

- Miller (1956): people hold about **7 ± 2** items in mind at once.[^miller]
- Cowan (2001): closer to **4 chunks** (3 to 5), once items cannot be rehearsed or grouped.[^cowan]
- A **chunk** is whatever is recognized as one unit: `for (var i = 0; i < n; i++)` is one chunk for an experienced programmer, but several for a beginner.

While reading code, every value to remember, every enclosing condition and every unfinished calculation takes one of those few slots.

[^miller]: G. A. Miller, ["The magical number seven, plus or minus two"](https://doi.org/10.1037/h0043158), Psychological Review, 1956.
[^cowan]: N. Cowan, ["The magical number 4 in short-term memory"](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X01003922), Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 2001.

### Essential and accidental complexity

Fred Brooks divided complexity into two kinds[^brooks]:

- **Essential** - comes from the problem. Experience rules with weekend bonuses, streaks and hint penalties are complex because the requirements are.
- **Accidental** - comes from how the solution is written: deep nesting, unclear names, a rule hidden in an unexpected place.

Essential complexity can only be organized. Accidental complexity can be removed.

[^brooks]: F. Brooks, ["No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering"](https://doi.org/10.1109/MC.1987.1663532), IEEE Computer, 1987 (first presented in 1986).

### Symptoms

Ousterhout lists three symptoms of complexity[^aposd-symptoms]:

- **Change amplification** - a simple change requires modifications in many places.
- **Cognitive load** - a lot has to be known to make a change.
- **Unknown unknowns** - it is not obvious what has to be changed, or what a change breaks.

[^aposd-symptoms]: J. Ousterhout, [*A Philosophy of Software Design*](https://web.stanford.edu/~ouster/cgi-bin/aposd.php), section 2.2 "Symptoms of complexity".

### Causes

Complexity is caused by **dependencies** (code cannot be understood or changed in isolation) and **obscurity** (important information is not obvious).[^aposd-causes] In code they look like:

[^aposd-causes]: J. Ousterhout, [*A Philosophy of Software Design*](https://web.stanford.edu/~ouster/cgi-bin/aposd.php), section 2.3 "Causes of complexity".

- deep nesting and long chains of conditions,
- long methods and long parameter lists, boolean flag parameters,
- shared mutable state and hidden inputs (the clock, files, static fields),
- the same decision repeated in many places,
- deep inheritance hierarchies and high coupling between classes,
- names that do not say what something is, or say something else.

| Completed within a minute without hints | +5 per word |
| Weekend | ×2 |
| Streak of 3+ days / 7+ days | +20 / +50 |
| First game of the day | +20 |
| Premium player | ×1.5, rounded down |
| Maximum | 200 |

### Lines of code

The simplest metric: the number of lines (usually without blank lines and comments).

- Easy to measure, and correlates with the number of defects.[^el-emam]
- Says nothing about structure: 60 lines of sequential code are simpler than 30 lines of nested conditions.
- Depends on formatting and style.

[^el-emam]: K. El Emam et al., ["The confounding effect of class size on the validity of object-oriented metrics"](https://doi.org/10.1109/32.935855), IEEE TSE, 2001: after controlling for size, many object-oriented metrics no longer predicted faults.

### Cyclomatic complexity

Thomas McCabe[^mccabe]: the number of linearly independent paths through a method.

- Counted as **decisions + 1**: every `if`, `case`, loop, `catch`, `&&`, `||` and `?:` adds one.
- In terms of the control flow graph: **E − N + 2**, where E is the number of edges and N the number of nodes.
- It is the minimum number of tests needed to run every branch at least once.

McCabe suggested 10 as the upper limit for a method.

[^mccabe]: T. McCabe, ["A Complexity Measure"](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.1976.233837), IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, 1976.

***

The streak bonus of `ExperienceCalculatorBefore`:

```csharp
if (completed.StreakDays > 0)
{
    if (completed.StreakDays >= 7) experience += 50;
    else if (completed.StreakDays >= 3) experience += 20;
}
```

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A{"StreakDays > 0"} -->|yes| B{">= 7"}
    A -->|no| E([end])
    B -->|yes| C["+50"]
    B -->|no| D{">= 3"}
    D -->|yes| F["+20"]
    D -->|no| E
    C --> E
    F --> E
```

3 decisions + 1 = 4. Graph: 8 edges − 6 nodes + 2 = 4.

### Cognitive complexity

Cyclomatic complexity counts paths, but not how hard they are to follow. *Cognitive complexity*[^cognitive] was designed to measure understandability:

- **+1** for every break in the linear flow: `if`, `else`, `switch`, loops, `catch`, sequences of `&&`/`||`, recursion.
- **+1 for every level of nesting** on top of that: an `if` inside a loop inside an `if` costs 3.
- Nothing for constructs that make code shorter to read, like `?.` and `??`.

[^cognitive]: G. Ann Campbell, ["Cognitive Complexity: A new way of measuring understandability"](https://www.sonarsource.com/docs/CognitiveComplexity.pdf), SonarSource white paper, 2017.

### Maintainability index

A single number from 0 to 100, as calculated by Visual Studio and rule [`CA1505`](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/fundamentals/code-analysis/quality-rules/ca1505)[^mi-vs]:

```text
MI = max(0, (171 − 5.2 × ln(Halstead volume) − 0.23 × cyclomatic complexity − 16.2 × ln(lines of code)) × 100 / 171)
```

*Halstead volume*[^halstead] measures the size of the code by the number of operators and operands it uses.

| Index | Visual Studio |
|---|---|
| 20 – 100 | good |
| 10 – 19 | moderate |
| 0 – 9 | low |

[^mi-vs]: Microsoft, ["Code metrics - Maintainability index range and meaning"](https://learn.microsoft.com/visualstudio/code-quality/code-metrics-maintainability-index-range-and-meaning).
[^halstead]: M. Halstead, *Elements of Software Science*, 1977; summary: [Halstead complexity measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halstead_complexity_measures).

### Coupling and cohesion

| Metric | Measures | .NET rule |
|---|---|---|
| Class coupling | How many other types a type or method uses | `CA1506` |
| Depth of inheritance | How many base classes a type has | `CA1501` |
| Afferent / efferent coupling | How many types use this one / are used by it | - |
| Instability | Efferent / (afferent + efferent): 0 is stable, 1 easy to change | - |
| Lack of cohesion (LCOM) | Whether methods of a class use the same fields | - |

Class coupling, depth of inheritance and LCOM are from the Chidamber & Kemerer suite[^ck]; afferent/efferent coupling and instability from Robert C. Martin[^martin].

[^ck]: S. Chidamber, C. Kemerer, ["A metrics suite for object oriented design"](https://doi.org/10.1109/32.295895), IEEE TSE, 1994.
[^martin]: R. C. Martin, *Agile Software Development: Principles, Patterns, and Practices*, 2002; summary: [Software package metrics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_package_metrics).

### Roslyn analyzers

The metrics in this lecture are measured by **Roslyn analyzers**: plugins of the C# compiler that inspect the code on every build and in the IDE. The ones used here are part of the .NET SDK (`Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.NetAnalyzers`).

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    Code[C# code] --> Compiler["Roslyn compiler<br/>syntax and operation trees"]

    Analyzers --> Warnings["Warnings in the build<br/>and in the IDE"]
```

| Metric | Rule |
|---|---|
| Cyclomatic complexity | `CA1502` |
| Maintainability index | `CA1505` |
| Class coupling | `CA1506` |
| Depth of inheritance | `CA1501` |

### Reducing complexity

The same rules, refactored:

```{.csharp include="09-construction/WordGame.Construction/Complexity/ExperienceCalculator.cs" region="after"}
```

***

What was done:

- **Guard clause** - the special case (no words) returns first, so the rest is not nested.
- **Extract method** - every rule got a name: `SpeedBonus`, `StreakBonus`.
- **Separate the order from the rules** - `Calculate` is the only place that says in which order the rules apply. That the weekend doubles the speed bonus, but not the streak bonus, is now visible in two lines.
- **Switch expressions instead of nested `if`s** - `StreakBonus` is a table, not a sequence of steps.

***

### Refactoring safely

Refactoring changes the structure of code without changing its behavior.[^refactoring] To know that the behavior did not change, it is pinned down by *characterization tests*[^characterization] **before** refactoring:

[^characterization]: M. Feathers, *Working Effectively with Legacy Code*, 2004, chapter 13; summary: [Characterization test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characterization_test).

## Anticipating and embracing change

### Information hiding

>Most software changes over time, and anticipating change drives many aspects of software construction.
>
>SWEBOK[^swebok-change]

David Parnas[^parnas]: divide a system into modules so that every module hides **a design decision that is likely to change**. When the decision changes, only that module changes.

[^swebok-change]: [SWEBOK Guide v4.0](https://www.computer.org/education/bodies-of-knowledge/software-engineering), section 4.1.2 "Anticipating and Embracing Change", p. 4-2.
[^parnas]: D. Parnas, ["On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules"](https://doi.org/10.1145/361598.361623), Communications of the ACM, 1972.

### Measuring change

The history in git shows where change actually happens:

- **Churn** - how often a file changes.
- **Hotspots** - files that are both complex and changed often. Complex code that never changes is not a problem; complex code changed every week is where effort pays off most.
- **Change coupling** - files that change in the same commits, which shows dependencies the code does not.

All three are described by Adam Tornhill.[^crime-scene]

[^crime-scene]: A. Tornhill, [*Your Code as a Crime Scene*](https://pragprog.com/titles/atcrime2/your-code-as-a-crime-scene-second-edition/), 2nd ed., 2024.

## Constructing for verification

>**Verification**: the process of evaluating a system or component to determine whether the products of a given development phase satisfy the conditions imposed at the start of that phase.
>
>IEEE 1012, quoted in SWEBOK[^swebok-vv]

[^swebok-vv]: [SWEBOK Guide v4.0](https://www.computer.org/education/bodies-of-knowledge/software-engineering), chapter 12 "Software Quality", section 3.4 "V&V and Testing", p. 12-12; from IEEE Std 1012-2016.

>Constructing for verification builds software in such a way that faults can be readily found by the software engineers writing the software as well as by the testers and users during independent testing and operational activities.
>
>SWEBOK[^swebok-verification]

Techniques: coding standards that support reviews and tests, code organized for automated testing, simple language constructs, logging.

[^swebok-verification]: [SWEBOK Guide v4.0](https://www.computer.org/education/bodies-of-knowledge/software-engineering), section 4.1.3 "Constructing for Verification", p. 4-4.

### Mutation testing

Test coverage shows which lines ran during the tests (see the [testing lecture](07-testing.qmd#measuring-test-coverage)), not whether the tests would notice a bug. Mutation testing measures that.

A mutation testing tool changes the code in small ways - `>=` to `>`, `+` to `-`, removes a statement - and runs the tests against every change (a *mutant*):

- If a test fails, the mutant is **killed**: the tests noticed the change.
- If all tests pass, the mutant **survived**: a bug like this would not be noticed.

**Mutation score** = killed mutants / all mutants.[^stryker]

[^stryker]: [Stryker Mutator documentation](https://stryker-mutator.io/docs/stryker-net/introduction/).

***

Three of the mutants Stryker.NET makes of `ExperienceCalculator`:

```diff
-        >= 7 => 50,
+        > 7 => 50,
```

Killed by the characterization tests: a 7-day streak now gets +20 instead of +50, so the expected 80 becomes 50.

```diff
-        experience += SpeedBonus(completed);
+        experience -= SpeedBonus(completed);
```

Survives the weak tests: the result is still between 1 and 200.

```diff
-        _ when hintsUsed >= wordCount => experience / 2,
+        _ when hintsUsed > wordCount => experience / 2,
```

Survives all tests: for three short words both branches give 15 (30 / 2 = 30 − 3 × 5).

***

Stryker.NET on `ExperienceCalculator`, once with each test project:

```{.text include="09-construction/reports/mutation.txt" region="score"}
```

▶ Run it from a test project's folder:

```bash
dotnet tool restore
dotnet stryker --test-runner mtp --project WordGame.Construction.csproj --mutate "**/Complexity/ExperienceCalculator.cs"
```

### Assertions and defensive programming

Where the input comes from decides how it is checked:

- **At a trust boundary** (an HTTP request, a file, user input) invalid input is expected: it is validated and rejected with an error the caller can act on (`400 Bad Request`).
- **Inside the application** invalid input means a bug in the caller: the method **fails fast**[^fail-fast] by throwing, so the bug is found where it is, not three calls later.

[^fail-fast]: J. Shore, ["Fail Fast"](https://doi.org/10.1109/MS.2004.1331296), IEEE Software, 2004.

```{.csharp include="07-testing/WordGame.Api/Users.cs" region="add-experience"}
```

## Reuse

>Reuse has two closely related facets: construction for reuse and construction with reuse. The former means creating reusable software assets, whereas the latter means reusing software assets to construct a new solution.
>
>SWEBOK[^swebok-reuse]

[^swebok-reuse]: [SWEBOK Guide v4.0](https://www.computer.org/education/bodies-of-knowledge/software-engineering), section 4.1.4 "Reusing Assets", p. 4-4.

### Measuring dependencies

Almost no software is written without libraries, and every library brings its own dependencies[^swebok-dependencies]:

[^swebok-dependencies]: Managing dependencies is a topic of its own in SWEBOK: [SWEBOK Guide v4.0](https://www.computer.org/education/bodies-of-knowledge/software-engineering), section 4.2.4 "Managing Dependencies", p. 4-5.

```{.text include="09-construction/reports/dependencies.txt" region="dependencies"}
```

***

```bash
# Every package, including the transitive ones
dotnet list package --include-transitive
# Packages with known vulnerabilities
dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive
# Packages with newer versions, and packages marked deprecated by their authors
dotnet list package --outdated
dotnet list package --deprecated
```

### Risks of reuse

- **Removed packages** - left-pad (2016): an 11-line npm package was unpublished, and builds all over the world broke.[^left-pad]
- **Malicious code** - the xz utils backdoor (2024) was planted by a maintainer who had gained trust over two years.[^xz]
- **Unexpected behavior** - Moq 4.20 (2023) shipped SponsorLink, which read the e-mail addresses of developers from their git configuration during build.[^moq]
- **License changes** - FluentAssertions 8 (2025) moved to a commercial license for commercial use.[^fluent-assertions]

[^left-pad]: [npm left-pad incident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Npm_left-pad_incident).
[^xz]: [XZ Utils backdoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XZ_Utils_backdoor).
[^moq]: [devlooped/moq#1372: Privacy issues with SponsorLink, starting from version 4.20](https://github.com/devlooped/moq/issues/1372).
[^fluent-assertions]: [fluentassertions/fluentassertions#2943: Update ownership and license](https://github.com/fluentassertions/fluentassertions/pull/2943).

### Construction for reuse

- **Duplication** is measured by clone detection: [jscpd](https://github.com/kucherenko/jscpd) (MIT license) reports the percentage of duplicated lines.
- **Rule of three**[^rule-of-three] - code is made reusable when it is needed for the third time, not the first: by then it is known which parts actually vary.
- **The wrong abstraction** - code shared between two places that later need different things grows flags and special cases.

>Duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction.
>
>Sandi Metz[^wrong-abstraction]

[^rule-of-three]: Attributed to Don Roberts in M. Fowler, [*Refactoring*](https://martinfowler.com/books/refactoring.html); summary: [Rule of three](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_three_(computer_programming)).
[^wrong-abstraction]: S. Metz, ["The Wrong Abstraction"](https://sandimetz.com/blog/2016/1/20/the-wrong-abstraction), 2016.

## Applying standards

SWEBOK lists the standards that directly affect construction[^swebok-standards]: communication methods (document formats), programming languages, coding standards (naming, layout), exception handling policies, platforms and tools. They are:

- **External** - programming languages, formats and protocols (OpenAPI, ISO 8601 dates), platform conventions ([.NET coding conventions](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/coding-style/coding-conventions)).
- **Internal** - the team's own: code style, how errors are handled, which libraries are used for what, how projects are structured.

[^swebok-standards]: [SWEBOK Guide v4.0](https://www.computer.org/education/bodies-of-knowledge/software-engineering), section 4.1.5 "Applying Standards in Construction", p. 4-4.

A standard that is not checked automatically is a suggestion. In .NET the build checks it.

### Standards enforced by the build

```{.xml include="09-construction/Directory.Build.props" region="standards"}
```

### Exceptions are decisions too

Every exception to a rule is written down with its reason:

```{.ini include="09-construction/.editorconfig" region="tests"}
```

```{.ini include="09-construction/.editorconfig" region="suppression"}
```

### Adopting standards in existing code

Turning on a rule in an existing codebase can produce hundreds of warnings. Instead of fixing all of them at once:

```{.ini include="09-construction/.editorconfig" region="baseline"}
```

## Summary

### Complexity metrics

| Metric | Shows | .NET tool | Gamed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lines of code | Size | any | formatting |
| Cyclomatic complexity | Paths, minimum tests | `CA1502` | splitting methods |
| Cognitive complexity | How hard code is to follow | - (counted by hand) | splitting methods |
| Maintainability index | Rough overall state | `CA1505` | short methods |
| Class coupling | Dependencies between types | `CA1506` | merging classes |

### Change, tests, reuse, standards

| Metric | Shows | Tool | Gamed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hotspots, change coupling | Where change happens | git history | rare, large commits |
| Coverage | Code the tests ran | Coverlet | tests without assertions |
| Mutation score | Whether tests notice bugs | Stryker.NET | equivalent mutants |
| Dependencies, vulnerabilities | Risk of reuse | `dotnet list package` | - |
| Warnings | Adherence to standards | Roslyn analyzers | suppressions |
